title: 道德經 第三十五章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 35, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 70. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 35 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 仁德 (Benevolent Potency). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: to grasp, to hold fast to
the Great Image — the Way considered as the one image behind all images; Wang Bi calls it 'the mother of the images of heaven'
great, large
an image, a likeness

sentences.l:
Hold fast the Great Image:
all-under-heaven goes to you.
sentences.i: Hold fast to the Great Image, and all under heaven will come over to you.
sentences.n: Nobody is named in either line. Classical Chinese requires no subject, and this book leaves the ruler to be understood almost every time it gives advice — the reader supplies him from the sense. 大象 is bound here as a single word because it is a name and not a description: 大 'great' plus 象 'an image' would leave you with a big picture, where Wang Bi means the one image that has no shape of its own and so can hold every shaped thing — it is neither cold nor hot, he says, neither warm nor cool, and therefore can wrap the ten thousand things round without injuring any of them. Chapter 41 uses the term again: 大象無形, 'the Great Image has no form'. 往 is plain motion, 'to go': the world goes to whoever holds it. English wants 'comes', which quietly moves the camera to where that man is standing, so the literal keeps 'goes' and only the idiomatic gives way.

morph.gloss: they go — the same character that closed the line before; Wang Bi supplies the subject it lacks, the ten thousand things
and yet, and even so
not
to harm, to do injury to
at rest, safe, unthreatened
level, even — nothing raised above anything else
utterly great, at the greatest ease; many editions print 泰 tài here, 'ease, tranquillity', and the two were interchangeable

sentences.l:
They go, and are not harmed:
at rest, level, great.
sentences.i: They come and take no hurt by it: safe, level, and at the height of ease.
sentences.n: Three stative verbs stacked with nothing to join them — 安平太, 'rest, level, great' — which is how this book habitually ends a thought, and a place where English must supply the commas the Chinese does not have. Wang Bi supplies the subject: the ten thousand things get to go to him and are neither harmed nor hindered. 太 is the hard character. It is the 太 of 太上 in chapter 17, 'the supreme'; but a number of editions print 泰 tài, 'ease, tranquillity', which sits better in a list of comforts, and in this period the two graphs were written for each other freely. Our text prints 太 and we keep it: the literal gives 太 its own sense, 'great', and the idiomatic pitches it as the height of ease, so the line can be heard either way.

sentences.t:
樂與餌，
過客止。
道之出口，
淡乎其無味，
視之不足見，
聽之不足聞，
用之不足既。

sentences.l:
Music and good food —
the passing traveller halts.
The Way's coming out of the mouth:
bland! — it has no flavour.
Look at it — not enough to see;
listen to it — not enough to hear;
use it — not enough to use up.
sentences.i: Music and a fine meal will halt a traveller in the road. But let the Way come out of a mouth and it is flat, with no savour in it. Look for it: there is not enough to see. Listen for it: not enough to hear. Use it: and there is never enough of it to use up.
sentences.n: The last three lines run one five-character frame three times without breaking it. 視之不足見 is a complaint — 'look at it: not enough to see'; 聽之不足聞 repeats the complaint; and 用之不足既, keeping every word in its place, turns the deficiency into the point. There is not enough of it to exhaust. Wang Bi reads it exactly so: what is not enough to please the eye or delight the ear is the very thing that cannot be used to the bottom. Two small things worth carrying away. 之 does two jobs inside this one unit, and only position tells them apart: the object pronoun 'it', three times over, and — in 道之出口 — a third job you have not met yet. There 之 stands between a subject and its verb and turns the whole clause into a noun: not 'the Way of coming out of the mouth' but 'the Way's coming out of the mouth'. It is not the genitive 'of' of chapter 1, though English translates both with an apostrophe. And 乎 is asking nothing here: you met it as the question particle, but standing after a single stative verb it is exclamatory, holding the word up — 淡乎, 'bland! —'. Sound: 餌 ěr and 止 zhǐ close the opening couplet and belonged to one Old Chinese rhyme group, so this was a rhyme; in Mandarin only a faint chime is left of it.
